t: LeetCode 2003 — Smallest Missing Genetic Value in Each Subtree
o:
## Understanding the problem

We must answer, for every node of a family tree rooted at 0, the smallest genetic value that is missing from that node's subtree (the node plus all descendants). Values are distinct integers drawn from 1 to 10^5, so each subtree misses some value in [1, n+1]. The decisive structural observation: an answer can exceed 1 only if the subtree contains the value 1. Since values are distinct, exactly one node carries value 1, so only that node and its ancestors need real computation — every other node answers 1 immediately.

Example walkthrough (parents = [-1,0,0,2], nums = [1,2,3,4]): node 3 (value 4) has a lone-node subtree missing 1; node 2's subtree holds {3,4}, node 1's holds {2} — both miss 1; node 0's subtree holds {1,2,3,4}, so its smallest missing value is 5. Output: [5,1,1,1].

Constraints: n up to 10^5 rules out collecting each subtree independently — on a path-shaped tree that costs O(n^2). We need total work that stays linear.
k: If value 1 is not inside a subtree, the answer is 1 — no search needed.
Values are distinct, so exactly one node carries value 1; only that node and its ancestors can have answers above 1.
Walking up from the value-1 node while growing one shared set lets the mex pointer advance monotonically, giving linear total time.

a.n: Approach 1: Collect each subtree independently (brute force)
a.i: For every node, traverse its entire subtree, put all values into a hash set, then scan upward from 1 until a value is absent. This mirrors the definition directly and is easy to get right. On a degenerated path tree each query costs O(n), so the whole run is O(n^2) — too slow at n = 10^5 but a correct baseline.
s: Build children adjacency lists from parents.
For each node i, traverse its subtree with a stack, inserting all visited values into a set.
Start mex = 1 and increment while mex lies in the set.
a.t: O(n^2) — each of the n subtrees may cost O(n) to collect (path tree worst case)
a.sp: O(n) — children lists plus the per-query set

a.n: Approach 2: Path walk with incremental mex (optimal)
a.i: Only ancestors of the value-1 node have answers above 1, so start there and walk up to the root. Maintain one global set of seen values; when reaching a new ancestor, push its untouched subtree onto a stack and insert its values (nodes already inserted are skipped, which keeps the total insertions linear). After absorbing each subtree, advance a monotone mex pointer until it escapes the set — because values only ever get added, the mex never needs to restart from 1.
s: Fill ans with 1 and locate the node holding value 1; if none exists, return immediately.
While the current node exists: traverse its not-yet-added subtree with a stack, marking nodes added and inserting their values into a shared set.
Advance mex while it is present in the set, then write mex as the answer for this node.
Move to parent[node]; stop after processing the root.

c.python:
class Solution:
    def smallestMissingValueSubtree(self, parents, nums):
        n = len(parents)
        children = [[] for _ in range(n)]
        for i in range(1, n):
            children[parents[i]].append(i)
        ans = [1] * n
        node = nums.index(1) if 1 in nums else -1
        if node == -1:
            return ans
        seen = set()
        added = [False] * n
        mex = 1
        while node != -1:
            stk = [node]
            while stk:
                u = stk.pop()
                if added[u]:
                    continue
                added[u] = True
                seen.add(nums[u])
                stk.extend(children[u])
            while mex in seen:
                mex += 1
            ans[node] = mex
            node = parents[node]
        return ans

a.t: O(n) — every node is inserted into the set exactly once over the whole walk, and the mex pointer only moves forward
a.sp: O(n) — children lists, seen set, and added marks

w:
## Wrap-up

In an interview, state the "no value 1 means answer 1" shortcut first, then describe Approach 2; keep Approach 1 in reserve to demonstrate you understand the definition. Pitfalls: naive recursion may overflow the call stack on a path tree of 10^5 nodes, so traverse iteratively; do not forget that non-ancestor nodes answer exactly 1; restarting the mex search from 1 at every ancestor still works but obscures the linear-time argument. Edge cases: value 1 entirely absent (all answers 1), value 1 sitting at the root, deep chains. Follow-ups: what if genetic values could repeat? Then many more subtrees contain 1 and heavier machinery such as small-to-large set merging becomes necessary.
